intro: Symmetric matrices, which mirror across their diagonal, have especially clean eigenvectors. This branch builds up to the singular value decomposition, a tool used in image compression and data science.

VII.9.01.what: A symmetric matrix equals its own mirror image across the diagonal. Such matrices have unusually well-behaved eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

levels.a: Recognizes a matrix that equals its own transpose.
levels.b: Learns that its eigenvalues are always real numbers.
levels.c: Learns its eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular.
levels.d: Works through examples to see these facts in action.

VII.9.02.what: Orthogonal diagonalization rewrites a symmetric matrix as pure stretches along perpendicular directions.

levels.a: Recognizes the form using a rotation-like matrix and its transpose.
levels.b: Builds that matrix from length-1 eigenvectors.
levels.c: Handles repeated eigenvalues by making their eigenvectors perpendicular.
levels.d: Checks the result by multiplying out.

VII.9.03.what: The spectral theorem guarantees every symmetric matrix can be broken into simple stretches along perpendicular directions.

levels.b: Writes the matrix as a sum of simple pieces, one per eigenvalue.
levels.c: Sees each piece as a scaled projection onto one direction.
levels.d: Explains why this result is so widely useful.

VII.9.04.what: A quadratic form is an expression where every term has two variables multiplied, like x squared plus 3xy. A matrix records it compactly.

levels.a: Writes a quadratic form using a symmetric matrix.
levels.b: Builds the matrix from a given expression.
levels.c: Changes variables to remove the mixed xy terms.
levels.d: Finds the main axes of the ellipse or other shape it describes.

VII.9.05.what: Definiteness says whether a quadratic form is always positive, always negative, or mixed, like a bowl, a dome or a saddle.

levels.a: Recognizes forms that are always positive (bowl-shaped).
levels.c: Decides which by checking the signs of the eigenvalues.
levels.d: Links this to finding maximums and minimums of surfaces.

VII.9.06.what: Finding the largest and smallest value of a quadratic form when the input must have length 1.

levels.a: Sets up the problem on a circle or sphere of radius 1.
levels.b: Shows the maximum equals the largest eigenvalue.
levels.c: Shows the minimum equals the smallest eigenvalue.
levels.d: Finds the directions where these extremes occur.

VII.9.07.what: Singular values measure how much any matrix, even a non-square one, stretches things in its main directions.

levels.a: Finds eigenvalues of the matrix's transpose times the matrix.
levels.b: Takes square roots of those to get the singular values.
levels.c: Interprets them as the stretch amounts in key directions.
levels.d: Finds the rank by counting nonzero singular values.

VII.9.08.what: The singular value decomposition (SVD) breaks any matrix into a rotation, a stretch and another rotation, used in data compression.

levels.a: Finds the first rotation from eigenvectors.
levels.b: Builds the middle stretch matrix from the singular values.
levels.c: Finds the final rotation from the other two.
levels.d: Checks that the three pieces multiply back to the original.
